reference.source: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology / Brenner and Rector's The Kidney
clinicalPearls: An acute kidney injury occurring in over-anticoagulated patients, classically with a supratherapeutic INR on warfarin, and also reported with direct oral anticoagulants
Thought to result from glomerular haemorrhage with red cells filling and obstructing the tubules as red-cell casts
Biopsy shows numerous red-cell casts occluding tubules with acute tubular injury, often on a background of pre-existing chronic kidney disease
Presents as an otherwise unexplained rise in creatinine coinciding with excessive anticoagulation, frequently with haematuria
Pre-existing renal disease, diabetes, hypertension and older age increase susceptibility
It is a diagnosis of exclusion after ruling out other causes of acute kidney injury and glomerular bleeding
Management is correction of over-anticoagulation, careful review of the need for and intensity of therapy, and supportive care, with biopsy reserved for uncertain cases
reference.pathophysiology: Anticoagulant-related nephropathy is proposed to arise when excessive anticoagulation permits bleeding across the glomerular filtration barrier, allowing red cells to pass into Bowman's space and the tubular lumina. The red cells aggregate with Tamm-Horsfall protein to form obstructing red-cell casts in the tubules, causing tubular obstruction, direct epithelial injury and reduced glomerular filtration. Underlying glomerular disease or endothelial and basement-membrane fragility, as in diabetes or hypertension, predisposes to this glomerular haemorrhage, explaining why it occurs largely in patients with pre-existing renal impairment. Oxidative tubular injury from haem and impaired repair in a chronically damaged kidney may compound the acute insult.
additionalDifferentials: Acute tubular injury from ischaemia or nephrotoxins
IgA nephropathy or other glomerular disease with macroscopic haematuria
additionalInvestigations: INR or anticoagulant activity level and review of anticoagulant dosing
Serial renal function and urinalysis with microscopy for red cells and red-cell casts
Exclusion of glomerulonephritis with relevant serology (ANCA, anti-GBM, complement)
Renal imaging to exclude obstruction and assess kidney size
Assessment of pre-existing chronic kidney disease and comorbidities
Renal biopsy in selected cases showing red-cell casts and tubular injury
redFlags: Marked or persistent supratherapeutic anticoagulation with rising creatinine
Heavy macroscopic haematuria or clot obstruction
Rapidly progressive renal failure prompting exclusion of glomerulonephritis
reference.prognosis: Anticoagulant-related nephropathy is associated with incomplete renal recovery, accelerated progression of underlying chronic kidney disease and increased mortality, particularly in those with pre-existing renal impairment. Prompt correction of over-anticoagulation and attention to comorbidities improve the chance of stabilising function, but a proportion sustain a permanent decline.
pitfalls: Overlooking excessive anticoagulation as the cause of unexplained acute kidney injury
Attributing haematuria solely to urological causes and missing glomerular bleeding
Failing to exclude a coexisting glomerulonephritis before ascribing injury to anticoagulation
Not reassessing the intensity and indication for anticoagulant therapy
Assuming full renal recovery once the INR is corrected
management: Correct over-anticoagulation promptly by withholding the anticoagulant and reversing warfarin with vitamin K or prothrombin complex concentrate according to the bleeding risk
Reassess the ongoing indication and target intensity of anticoagulation, tighten monitoring and consider switching agent to minimise recurrence
Provide supportive acute kidney injury care by avoiding nephrotoxins, optimising volume status and renal perfusion, and dose-adjusting renally cleared drugs
Manage the underlying chronic kidney disease and its drivers, controlling blood pressure and diabetes and using renin-angiotensin blockade where appropriate
Exclude and treat other causes of glomerular haematuria and acute kidney injury, since this remains a diagnosis of exclusion supported by biopsy in selected cases
Monitor renal function and urinalysis serially and provide renal replacement therapy if injury is severe
Refer to nephrology for ongoing assessment and management
